stem: A 44-year-old man comes to the clinic for a follow-up evaluation 6 months after successful antibiotic treatment for infective endocarditis.  The patient has no symptoms and reports good exercise tolerance.  Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 140/62 mm Hg, and pulse is 82/min.  Chest auscultation reveals a decrescendo diastolic murmur over the third intercostal space along the left sternal border.  Echocardiogram confirms severe aortic regurgitation.  Which of the following changes is most likely responsible for maintaining cardiac output in this patient?​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌

options.label: E
options.text: Increase in left ventricular stroke volume

explanation:
This patient has developed chronic aortic regurgitation (AR) as a consequence of infective endocarditis.  Incomplete closure of the aortic valve allows blood ejected during systole to flow back into the left ventricle during diastole; in severe AR, this regurgitant volume is ≥50% of total left ventricular stroke volume.  Because the left ventricle fills from both the left atrium and the aorta during diastole, left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV) increases (volume overload), which triggers eccentric hypertrophy with compensatory dilation of the ventricular chamber.  This response causes an increase in total stroke volume that offsets the regurgitant volume, maintaining forward stroke volume (ie, the net volume delivered to the systemic circulation) and cardiac output.  The large stroke volume ejected into the aorta also raises systolic blood pressure, and backflow into the left ventricle lowers diastolic blood pressure, producing widened pulse pressure.

The compensatory eccentric hypertrophy in chronic AR can eventually become maladaptive.  Progressive left ventricular dilation increases wall stress, leading to contractile dysfunction and ultimately left ventricular failure.

(Choice A)  Concentric hypertrophy occurs with ventricular pressure overload (eg, hypertension, aortic stenosis); it involves ventricular wall thickening without chamber enlargement, which allows the ventricle to generate higher systolic pressures.  In contrast, the predominant change in AR is eccentric hypertrophy.

(Choice B)  In AR, left ventricular preload or LVEDV is increased, rather than decreased.  This helps the ventricle maintain cardiac output via the Frank-Starling mechanism.  Decreased preload would cause a reduction in cardiac output.

(Choice C)  Aortic elasticity is the ability of the aortic wall to stretch during systole and recoil during diastole; greater elasticity corresponds to greater compliance.  Aortic stiffening (ie, decreased elasticity) occurs with aging and results in higher systolic blood pressure with widened pulse pressure.  Although chronic AR also causes widened pulse pressure, this results from increased stroke volume and diastolic regurgitation, not a change in aortic elasticity.

(Choice D)  Afterload is the left ventricular wall stress during systolic ejection; it rises with higher intraventricular pressure and larger chamber radius.  Although diastolic blood pressure is low in chronic AR, overall afterload is increased due to the enlarged chamber radius and the elevated systolic pressure.  Increased afterload opposes ejection rather than helping maintain cardiac output.

(Choice F)  Because cardiac output is maintained by an increase in stroke volume, there is typically minimal increase in heart rate in compensated chronic AR.  However, in acute AR, the absence of eccentric hypertrophy limits the capacity to increase stroke volume; therefore, compensatory tachycardia becomes important for maintaining cardiac output.

Educational objective:In chronic aortic regurgitation, persistent left ventricular volume overload triggers eccentric hypertrophy, which causes a compensatory increase in total stroke volume that offsets the regurgitant volume and maintains forward cardiac output.  This compensatory mechanism allows for a relatively long asymptomatic period in most patients.​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌
